To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the revised criteria for probable AD dementia include: a history of progressive cognitive decline; evidence of impairment in at least two cognitive domains; and the absence of a major confusional condition.

probable AD dementia is a diagnosis based primarily on a clinical assessment of memory impairment plus one additional cognitive impairment, with no disturbance of consciousness and no disturbance of motor or sensory function.

(1) the clinical diagnosis of AD dementia is made on the basis of a careful history, a physical and neurological examination, and neuropsychological testing; (2) biomarker evidence is used to support the clinical diagnosis of probable or possible AD dementia in research settings and in clinical practice; and (3) the diagnosis of AD should be made on the basis that the dementia syndrome is most likely due to AD and that all other causes of dementia have been excluded by appropriate clinical investigation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of biomarkers to detect the earliest signs of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and the development of a blood test that could be used in the diagnosis of AD.
understanding the mechanisms of the disease, developing biomarkers, and identifying effective interventions.
the identification and treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the clinical diagnosis of AD dementia is based on the core clinical criteria, which are the clinical presentation of a progressive dementia, and the presence of a decline in at least one domain of cognitive function, with the exclusion of other causes of dementia.
the diagnosis of AD is based on the clinical presentation of dementia and evidence from biomarkers.
the diagnosis of AD is a clinical diagnosis based on the history, physical examination, and cognitive and functional assessments that can be supported by biomarker evidence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we now have a set of criteria that will allow the clinician to diagnose AD dementia with a high level of confidence in the majority of cases and to identify a subset of individuals with AD dementia for whom biomarker data are available.

the revised criteria for probable AD dementia will continue the clinical framework of 1984, but with a greater focus on the core clinical features of episodic memory impairment and the temporal profile of decline.
the clinical diagnosis of probable AD dementia is the same as before, but the clinical diagnosis of possible AD dementia is now a more focused concept.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the revised criteria for AD dementia should be viewed as the beginning, not the end, of a process to develop the most accurate and useful clinical diagnostic criteria for AD dementia.
the clinical diagnosis of AD dementia remains central and will continue to be refined.
the diagnosis of AD is evolving from a purely clinical diagnosis to one that integrates biomarker evidence with the clinical picture.
